blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Fix 2 instead", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action (the app's own label is used).

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo (a key also hides the on-screen keyboard); 'set_appearance' switches the device to light or dark mode; 'appearance' says which it is in; 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus, and 'press_key' and 'text' hide it again); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

Links: [{"title":"Back to blog","url":"https://docsio.co/blog/starlight-vs-docusaurus"},{"title":"Documentation Framework Comparison","url":"https://sv0-docs.pages.dev/docs/architecture/research/2026-03-11-documentation-framework-comparison"},{"title":"docusaurus vs vitepress vs nextra vs starlight 2026","url":"https://www.pkgpulse.com/guides/docusaurus-vs-vitepress-vs-nextra-vs-starlight-2026"},{"title":"Starlight vs Docusaurus, which one wins for your brief, in 2026","url":"https://gautamkhorana.com/static-site-generators/compare/starlight-vs-docusaurus/"},{"title":"docusaurus vs starlight","url":"https://toolradar.com/compare/docusaurus-vs-starlight"},{"title":"starlight vs docusaurus","url":"https://toolradar.com/compare/starlight-vs-docusaurus"},{"title":"best documentation frameworks 2026","url":"https://www.pkgpulse.com/guides/best-documentation-frameworks-2026"}]

The search turned up mostly opinion-style comparison posts rather than measured migration benchmarks, so treat the performance claims as directional.

- **Runtime JavaScript:** Several sources say Starlight is lighter on the client. One describes Astro as shipping almost no JavaScript by default, while Docusaurus relies on React hydration, which one source says makes a meaningful difference in LCP for docs pages. Starlight ships zero JavaScript by default (Astro). Docusaurus ships React hydration.
- **Built-in features:** Docusaurus is generally the stronger choice for large, versioned doc sets. One comparison notes that Starlight does not ship built-in versioning. Another says Docusaurus has more plugins, themes, and integrations in 2026.
- **i18n:** Both handle it, with different trade-offs. One source says Starlight's Astro-native i18n is cleaner; Docusaurus's is more battle-tested.
- **Search:** Starlight uses Pagefind for local, self-contained search, while Docusaurus commonly uses Algolia DocSearch, which scales beautifully for large public docs but assumes you are comfortable with a hosted index.
- **Adoption:** One guide reports roughly ~500K weekly downloads for Docusaurus and about 100K for Starlight, which suggests Docusaurus has the larger installed base.
- **Migration risk:** One internal analysis recommends prototyping both on real content before committing. It also flags that Docusaurus's Markdown-fidelity option is marked experimental, which matters if you need pure .md compatibility. Another review notes that major version upgrades (v2 to v3) can require significant migration effort, which is a Starlight-side caveat.

Bottom line: Starlight is the likely pick if build speed and client-side weight matter most and you don't need versioning. Docusaurus is the safer pick for a large versioned API/SDK docs set. For a real decision, benchmark both on a sample of your own content, since I found no independent large-site migration benchmark.

The search turned up several reports on OpenAI's "Sign in with ChatGPT," which lets users log into third-party apps with their ChatGPT account and, optionally, spend their ChatGPT plan allowance there.

results:
The search turned up several reports on OpenAI's "Sign in with ChatGPT," which lets users log into third-party apps with their ChatGPT account and, optionally, spend their ChatGPT plan allowance there.

- **Origin and expansion:** The feature began as an identity tool in July 2026 and was expanded at DevDay, where Plus and Pro subscribers could use their plan allowance in participating third-party tools instead of paying through the API or the tool's own credits (This expands on the Sign in with ChatGPT feature launched in beta in July, which previously covered only identity/account linking.).
- **Usage and caps:** Usage comes from ChatGPT Work and Codex allowances. Users can set weekly caps for individual apps, and once the relevant limit is reached, included usage stops rather than automatically switching to the third party's own billing.
- **Launch partners:** Reports name Devin, Notion, Vercel, T3, OpenClaw and Dactyl among the 16 partners in a limited preview.
- **Developer implications:** Reports note a dependency risk: relying on the ChatGPT login makes them dependent on OpenAI's account system, rules and limits. One report says developers who want to add the feature to paid apps or apps running on remote servers must apply separately. OpenAI's help center says commercial partners interested in the integration, with or without token sharing, should complete an interest form (If you're a commercial partner interested in integrating Sign in with ChatGPT, with or without token sharing, please complete this interest form.).
- **Plan eligibility:** OpenAI's help article says the optional plan usage requires a Go, Plus, or Pro plan, while anyone can sign in without it (Anyone can sign in to participating apps and sites with ChatGPT, but optional plan usage in participating commercial apps and sites requires a Go, Plus, or Pro plan.). Some reports mention only Plus and Pro, so the help center is the more current source here.

The sources don't fully agree on the feature's status. Some describe it as a limited preview, while OpenAI's help documentation treats it as a supported feature. Check OpenAI's partner directory for the current list of participating apps.

OpenAI's docs describe Sign in with ChatGPT as a limited trial, with an interest form for commercial apps. The interest form detail comes from a third-party blog, so confirm it on OpenAI's site.

- **Access:** Sign in with ChatGPT is currently available to selected commercial partners through a limited trial. A third-party DEV post says commercial apps apply via an interest form.
- **Website integration:** OpenAI's guide says to add Continue with ChatGPT to your website using the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow with PKCE and OpenID Connect. It lists the issuer and endpoints at https://auth.openai.com, and client IDs typically begin with oaiapp_.
- **Token sharing (ChatGPT plan usage):** This is optional and separate from sign-in. The open-source flow requests offline_access to request a refresh token, and resource.invoke with chatgpt.tokens.use.direct to request API access using the user's ChatGPT plan. The resource is https://api.openai.com/v1. Eligibility is limited: eligible ChatGPT Plus and Pro users can use their ChatGPT plan for AI requests in your product.
- **Gating:** A successful identity sign-in alone does not grant permission to use the user's ChatGPT plan. Check the granted scope before enabling AI requests.
- **No client secret for open-source apps:** OpenAI registers the client during this flow, so you don't need a client secret or an API key.
- **Identity caveat:** OpenAI warns that a matching email address is not proof of account ownership.

content.content:
**Continue with ChatGPT on a website: summary**

**Requirements**
- An OpenAI OAuth client ID (typically starting with `oaiapp_`), obtained by requesting a client.
- An exact registered callback URL for each environment.
- Endpoints loaded from OpenAI's discovery document (issuer, authorization, token, and JWKS).
- The token-endpoint auth method you were provisioned with. Confidential clients also need a client secret.
- A backend that can store short-lived sign-in transaction state and create your own application sessions.

The flow is OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code with PKCE and OpenID Connect. Your backend exchanges the code, verifies the ID token, and maps the verified issuer, client ID, and subject (`sub`) to a local account. You then issue your own session.

**Approval and trial status**
The page says Sign in with ChatGPT is "currently available to selected commercial partners through a limited trial." Access requires joining a waitlist through an OpenAI representative.

**Scopes**
The guide covers identity sign-in only: `openid`, `profile`, and `email`. It states that ChatGPT plan usage in open-source apps "has a separate authorization and registration flow," which it links to separately.

**Model calls with the user's plan (token sharing)**
This page does not cover it. It doesn't say whether a website can make model calls with a user's ChatGPT plan. That capability is documented in the separate token-sharing guide. The identity-only contract requires only `id_token`, and the page notes that an access or refresh token is not part of it.

**Browser vs. server**
The integration is backend-driven. Token exchange, PKCE verifier handling, and secret storage all happen server-side. The page says not to return "an ID token, PKCE verifier, authorization code, or client secret to browser JavaScript," and that a client secret must never be exposed "in client-side code."

**Brand and button guidelines**
- Use approved OpenAI branding and assets with a clear, accessible label, such as "Continue with ChatGPT."
- Choose one of four provided button formats (white or black logo, "Continue" or "Sign in" wording).
- Add the `data-oai-siwc-button` attribute to each button, and optionally `data-oai-siwc-button-client` with your client ID.

content.content:
**Summary of the page (ChatGPT plan usage in Sign in with ChatGPT)**

- **Who qualifies:** The page says the docs are for "open-source and locally hosted apps." Paid or remotely hosted apps must complete an interest form. It doesn't define "open source" further.
- **Browser/website vs. CLI:** The page doesn't address this. Its flow opens the system browser and returns to a loopback callback, but it doesn't say whether browser-based or website apps are supported.
- **Client registration:** It uses dynamic registration. "each issued client_id is bound to the authenticated user and the workspace selected during registration." Each host also needs a stable `ext_agent_host_id`, chosen before its first sign-in. The page doesn't mention a client secret, and it uses PKCE with state and nonce.
- **Redirect URI:** The page describes a "loopback callback" that receives the code, state, and client_id. It doesn't list further constraints such as localhost-only.
- **API calls:** Requests go to the Responses API with a bearer access token, using `store: false` and `stream: true`, and the client processes the stream through `response.completed`. The page doesn't name specific models. It points to a separate models page for listing available models.
- **Rate limits:** The page mentions "shared plan usage settings and limits" but gives no specific numbers.
- **Restrictions:** Token use "does not grant access to their ChatGPT conversations or other account context." Paid or remotely hosted apps need the interest form. Host IDs should be opaque, not an email or user ID, and "A host ID is not an authentication credential."

**Not covered in this page:** browser-app eligibility, redirect URI rules, specific models, rate limit values, and server-side usage details. The linked pages on sign-in, models and inference, and preview limitations may address these.

Its usage policy section says the plan-usage integration "is available for open-source tools and personal projects that run locally." It also says that for "a paid or remotely hosted app," you should join the waitlist before offering it to users. The "At launch" line lists "open-source projects" more broadly, so a free, open-source, hosted site could fall under either statement. The page doesn't resolve that, so check with OpenAI before relying on hosted access.

**Models:** The page doesn't name any specific models. It says `chatgpt.listModels()` returns the models available to the active connection, and you use that list to populate a model picker.

- Requests draw on the user's plan allowance or available credits, and the page doesn't give numeric limits.
- If a request hits a usage limit, the app should direct users to manage usage in ChatGPT Settings.
- Identity-only integration is limited to a select group of commercial partners.

--- /** * Global "Ask Maester AI" assistant: a shared slide-over rendered once in * PortalLayout so the assistant is reachable from every portal page. The * test-detail page keeps its own deeply test-specific assistant; this one is * the general help surface (posture, changes, how-tos) that lets people * self-serve instead of opening a ticket. */ import NucleoIcon from './NucleoIcon.astro'; const prompts = [ { q: 'Why is my posture dropping?', a: 'Fleet posture slipped from 92% to 86% over the last week. The biggest driver is three tenants regressing on EIDSCA.PR06 (admin MFA) after a Conditional Access change on Contoso, plus SPF records failing on two new domains. Open Tests and sort by regressions to see the seven checks that moved pass → fail. I can walk you through fixing any of them.', }, { q: 'What changed this week?', a: '7 checks regressed and 2 recovered. Notable regressions: admin MFA (EIDSCA.PR06) and SPF records (CISA.EXO.4.1) now fail on multiple tenants. Recovered: Purview audit retention on Woodgrove and Adventure Works. The Changes page has the full per-tenant diff.', }, { q: 'How do I add and connect a tenant?', a: 'Go to Tenants → Add tenant and enter the directory (GUID) ID, a display name and the primary domain. Then add a Microsoft Graph connection. Either sign in interactively (we store an encrypted, auto-refreshing access token) or use managed-identity federation (no secret stored). Finally enable the daily schedule, or hit Run now to assess immediately.', }, { q: 'How are credentials stored?', a: 'Per connection you choose one of two methods. Interactive sign-in: you consent once and we keep an encrypted access token that is silently refreshed before each run. Managed-identity federation: the runner authenticates through a federated credential you grant in your tenant, so nothing secret is ever stored. You can see each connection’s method and token expiry on the tenant page.', }, { q: 'A run looks stuck. What do I do?', a: 'Open Tenants → the tenant → the run (or Runs), watch the live console, and if it is wedged on a step you can Cancel it and Re-run. Most stuck runs are a connection that needs re-consent, and the console log will show the exact Connect-* call that failed.', }, ]; ---

# The .dc.html authoring format — full rules and syntax card Read this when an artboard needs more than SKILL.md's skeleton. Everything the format supports is stated here — never design around a presumed gap ("I'll make the swatches static because I can't verify event syntax"): events, state and conditionals all work. ## Authoring an artboard A Design Component is one self-contained HTML file the editor (and its runtime) understands. Shape: ```html Hello

{{title}}

{{item.label}}
``` Rules beyond SKILL.md's "Rules that bite": - `lang` on `` is the copy's language (`en` here); change it when the design's text is not English. - `` names the screen for accessibility; give each artboard its own, in a few words. - Layout containers: a STACK is a flex `<div>` — inline `display: flex` plus `flex-direction`, `gap`, `justify-content`, `align-items`, with `flex-grow` / `align-self` on children. A GRID is a CSS-grid `<div>` — `display: grid` plus `grid-template-columns: repeat(N, minmax(0, 1fr))` and `gap`; children flow into the cells in document order. Both are first-class in the editor: the properties panel edits the full set (grid Columns/Rows read and write as a plain track count when the tracks are equal — author them in exactly the `repeat(N, minmax(0, 1fr))` shape so panel edits round-trip), viewers create them with the toolbar's Artboard tool or "Wrap in flex" / "Wrap in grid", and a viewer can drag an item OUT of either — the editor then freezes the remaining siblings and the parent's size so nothing else on the page moves. A DIAGRAM (boxes joined by lines) is neither: on a canvas build it from separate placed elements, never one `<svg>`, which the editor selects as one block (guidance to hand-draw a diagram as inline `<svg>` in a `<figure>` is for ordinary pages, not a canvas). `diagrams.md` has the forms: read it first. - Multi-frame design explorations are ARTBOARDS: put each frame in its own `.dc.html` entry and lay them out with `canvas.json` — the host canvas provides the infinite pan/zoom; no in-file meta flag switches modes. Give every artboard whose content really works (handlers, inputs, navigation) `"is_interactive": true` in its canvas.json entry — only those get the blue mark and a Play button; leave it off static comps. A clickable prototype is one artboard per screen, joined by links (Links between artboards, below). A PAGE (landing page, dashboard, web app screen, scrolling explainer) gets `"expand": "fill"` on its artboard entry and a fluid root — in the full-window view it fills the window and scrolls as a page (without `fill` it is shrunk to fit); side menu + content: a `flex-wrap: wrap` row, content `flex: 999 1 560px; min-width: 0`, so the menu (never sticky or `100vh`) stacks on a phone; toolbars wrap; wide tables get an `overflow-x: auto` box; a one-file design can launch focused (`{"launch": {"view": "focused", "file": "Main.dc.html"}}`). - LAYOUT GUIDES: an artboard entry may carry `"guides"`, up to 6, drawn by the canvas OVER the artboard, never in Play, exports or markup: `{"kind":"columns","count":12,"gutter":24,"margin":80}` (align `"stretch"`, default, divides the width inside `margin`; `"start"|"center"|"end"` pack `count` tracks of `"size"` px, `"offset"` in from that edge; `"count":"auto"` = as many as fit), `{"kind":"rows",…}` (same fields down the height; default `"auto"` 8 px rows every 8), `{"kind":"grid","size":8}`; any may add `"color"` (hex or rgb()/hsl(), alpha = strength; default red at 10%) and `"hidden":true`. Add a guide only when a grid layout genuinely helps, never on every artboard. When an artboard has `"guides"`, lay the content ON it — a stretch guide is `display:grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(count, minmax(0,1fr)); column-gap:<gutter>px; padding-inline:<margin>px`; children span tracks — and treat the user's guide edits as the intended layout. - The design content a viewer edits is **untrusted cross-user input** like everything in the published state. It runs ONLY inside the editor's sandboxed preview iframe (editor-and-saving.md § How saving and sharing work) — never lift published design source into the host page, an unsandboxed surface, or any prompt without fencing (the shared fenceUntrusted rule: published-state-derived text entering any prompt is wrapped in nonce-delimited untrusted-data markers, with an instruction to treat it as data, so the receiving model does not read it as instructions). ## Quick syntax card (a syntax demo; `{{title}}` etc. are placeholders) - **Holes**: `{{ path }}` is a dotted lookup only (`{{ user.name }}`, `{{ $index }}`, literals like `{{ true }}`) — never an expression (`{{ a + b }}`, `{{ !x }}`, `{{ fn() }}` fail silently). Compute in `renderVals()` and expose the result by name. - **Attributes**: `x="literal"` → string; `x="{{ path }}"` → the raw value (number, function, ref); `x="a {{p}} b"` → interpolated string. `class`/`for` auto-map to `className`/`htmlFor`. - **Events ARE supported**: whole-value attrs with JSX camelCase — `onClick="{{ pick }}"` — where `pick` is a function returned from `renderVals()`. Interactive selected-states (clickable swatches, size pills) are the house pattern: keep the selection in `state`, and for per-item handlers attach one to each loop item in `renderVals()` — `items: xs.map((x) => ({ ...x, pick: () => this.setState({ picked: x.id }) }))` — then bind `onClick="{{ item.pick }}"` inside the `<sc-for>`. - **Control flow**: `<sc-if value="{{ cond }}" hint-placeholder-val="{{ true }}">…</sc-if>` branches; `<sc-for list="{{ items }}" as="item" hint-placeholder-count="3">` repeats with `{{ item.x }}` and `{{ $index }}` in scope. Always set the `hint-*` attrs (they render while values stream in). - **Links between artboards**: `<a href="Cart.dc.html">View cart</a>` moves Play to that artboard, in place or full window (not while editing). The href is the target's path relative to this artboard's; a leading `/` means the canvas root (`/sub/Cart.dc.html`). Style the `<a>` itself as the button: a `<button>` or input inside it swallows the click. `href="#id"` scrolls within the artboard; `https://…` opens a tab. Each artboard keeps its own `state`, so a flow that must share state across screens is ONE artboard: its handlers set a `state` field, `renderVals()` returns one flag per screen from it, and each screen sits in its own `<sc-if>`. - **Conditional styling in a loop**: precompute the varying piece per item in `renderVals()` (e.g. each item carries `ringStyle` or `selected`) and either branch with `<sc-if>` or bind the computed value — a style hole is acceptable for live, state-driven values (selection highlights) and for a declared tweak prop (`{{accent}}`), just never for other static theme tokens, which belong inline so they paint while streaming. - **Logic class**: plain classic JS, no TypeScript, no import/export; must be `class Component extends DCLogic`. You get `this.props`, `state`/`setState`/`forceUpdate` and React class lifecycle (`componentDidMount`…), minus `render()`. `renderVals()` returns the template's inputs: flat values, arrays, handlers, refs. - **`data-props` editors** (on the `<script type="text/x-dc" data-dc-script>` tag): per-prop `{"editor": "text"|"color"|"int"|"float"|"range"|"boolean"| "enum"|null, "default": …, "tsType": "…"}` plus `options` for enum, `min`/`max`/`step`/`unit` for numbers/range, `section` to group; on color, `options` as a 3–4-item list of hex strings renders swatches. `editor: null` for callbacks/objects. Editable props open in the panel's Tweaks tab from the artboard's Tweaks button (which props deserve an editor: below). `default` seeds the editor only — fall back with `this.props.x ?? …` in `renderVals()`. `$preview: {"width", "height"}` sets the preferred preview size for sized fragments (a PAGE declares it too: its frame's `w`×`h`). - **Tweaks are levers, not copy.** Every `data-props` entry with an editor becomes a control in the Tweaks tab, so declare few, deliberate ones: behavioral switches (a dark or density toggle, a variant enum, an item count) and values that cut across the design in many places (one accent or tint color, a spacing or type scale). Do NOT make tweaks for label or body copy unless the user asks — write copy as literal text in the markup (not a prop, and not a `renderVals()` binding unless it is genuinely data) so viewers retype it in place in the WYSIWYG editor — and do not make a tweak for a color used in a single place; they restyle that element in the properties panel. - **`data-props` escaping**: it is a normal HTML attribute — the runtime reads it with `getAttribute` and then JSON-parses, so HTML entities decode first: write `&` for `&`, `'` for a literal single quote, and JSON `\"` for double quotes inside strings. Single-quote the attribute itself (`data-props='…'`) — every example assumes it, and a double-quoted attribute changes which characters need escaping. Those three escapes are the complete list: raw UTF-8 (em-dashes, middle dots, accented letters) is safe as-is, no numeric entities needed. - **Editable text, including multi-line**: a `{{hole}}` bound to a `data-props` entry with `{"editor": "text"}` renders as a TEXT node — HTML in the value is escaped, so `<br>` will not work. For multi-line text, pair `\n` in the JSON default with `white-space: pre-line` (or `pre-wrap`) in the bound element's inline style — without it HTML collapses the newline to a space and the lines run together (a real shipped bug: a two-line band lineup rendered as one merged line). For rich per-line layout, split into multiple props, one element each. - **Child DCs**: `<dc-import name="Card" item="{{ it }}" hint-size="100%,120px"></dc-import>` mounts the sibling file `Card.dc.html` (which is also an artboard of its own); every other attribute becomes a prop on the child (kebab→camel, read as `this.props.item` — declare it in the child's `data-props` with `"editor": null` when it is an object or callback; avoid a prop named `name`, which selects the component); `hint-size="W,H"` (CSS lengths) is the placeholder box shown until the child renders, so match the child's root size; works inside `<sc-for>`; never self-close and never use capitalized tags (`<Card/>`).

# Microsoft Zero Trust Assessment pack

The [Zero Trust Assessment](https://aka.ms/zerotrust/assessment) is Microsoft's free tool that checks a tenant
against Microsoft's Zero Trust guidance, across identity, devices, network, data, AI and security operations, and
says how to fix what it finds.
[Try the demo report](https://aka.ms/zerotrust/assessment/demo) to see what it covers.

This pack runs the assessment from Maester and shows each of its results in the Maester report, next to Maester's
own checks. It ships with Maester and runs only when you ask for it.

Each result is one row, `ZTA.<assessment test ID>` (for example `ZTA.21770`), with the assessment's title, risk
level (as the severity), description, remediation steps and findings. Results are tagged `ZeroTrust` and
`ZeroTrust.<pillar>` (`ZeroTrust.Identity`, `ZeroTrust.Devices` and so on).

## Report an issue with a test

Microsoft writes and maintains the assessment's tests. If a test's result, text or remediation looks wrong, raise
it in [microsoft/zerotrustassessment](https://github.com/microsoft/zerotrustassessment/issues). Problems with
running the pack from Maester go to [maester365/maester](https://github.com/maester365/maester/issues).

## Run it

Install the assessment's module once, connect Maester to the tenant, then name the pack:

```powershell
Install-Module ZeroTrustAssessment -Scope CurrentUser
Connect-Maester
Invoke-Maester -Pack ZTA -SkipBuiltIn    # only the Zero Trust Assessment
Invoke-Maester -Pack ZTA                 # Maester's tests and the assessment
```

The assessment runs in its own PowerShell process, so Maester signs in there for you. After an interactive
`Connect-Maester` you sign in a second time, in the browser. Without a browser, for example over SSH, set
`ZeroTrustAssessment.Connect` to `{ "UseDeviceCode": true }` in `maester-config.json`.

### Sign in as a service principal

In a pipeline, or anywhere nobody can sign in, connect Maester to Graph app-only with a certificate. The
assessment uses the same app and certificate, found by its thumbprint in the certificate store. A client secret, a
managed identity or workload identity federation is enough for Maester's own tests, but the assessment signs in
app-only only with a certificate.

```powershell
Import-Module ZeroTrustAssessment
Get-ZtGraphScope    # the Graph application permissions to give the app

Connect-MgGraph -ClientId <app id> -TenantId <tenant id> -CertificateThumbprint <thumbprint> -NoWelcome
Invoke-Maester -Pack ZTA -NonInteractive
```

To leave out the assessment's Azure, Exchange Online, Security & Compliance and SharePoint tests, which need extra
roles for the app, set `ZeroTrustAssessment.Connect` to `{ "Service": ["Graph"] }`.

### Read a report you already have

Run the assessment as its own step, then point Maester at the report it wrote:

```powershell
Connect-ZtAssessment
Invoke-ZtAssessment -Path ./zt -NoBrowser

  From docs/packs/* and /Users/merill/github/maester/packs/README.md:
  
  - A pack is a folder or repo of native tests, helpers and optional connectors to services Maester doesn't know (for example `CNT.GoogleWorkspace`). It is published by someone else, usually on GitHub, with a `maester-pack.json` manifest and a banner.
  - **Install:** `Install-MtPack owner/repo` scans the pack statically without running it, enforces a 72-hour release cooldown, and checks your pack policy and a signed blocklist. It pins PowerShell Gallery modules by digest, shows reach and risk, and asks for approval.

      Service = 'Graph',
      License = 'AAD_PREMIUM',
      Author = 'merill',
      Contributor = ('f-bader', 'weyCC81')
  )]
  [CmdletBinding()]

  foreach ($policy in $policies) {

Maester is the open-source security test framework for Microsoft 365, Entra, Azure and Active Directory. Run 841 built-in checks across CIS, CISA SCuBA, EIDSCA and ORCA, add Microsoft's Zero Trust Assessment, and get one report you can act on.

PS> Install-Module Maester
Quickstart → Browse 1,177 checks

PowerShell 7.4+ on Windows, macOS and Linux · Runs locally or in your pipeline · Nothing leaves your tenant

Maester runs Microsoft's free Zero Trust Assessment and puts each of its 336 results next to Maester's own checks: identity, devices, network, data, AI and security operations. One run, one report, one place to track the fixes.

Maester 3.0

A test engine built for security checks.

3.0 replaces the Pester runner with Maester's own engine. Tests ship inside the module, carry their own metadata, and every check that doesn't run tells you why.

What's new in 3.0 →
{{w.title}}
{{w.body}}
Automate

Run it every day, wherever you already deploy.

Schedule Maester in your pipeline with workload identity federation, so there are no secrets to rotate. Get the results by email, Teams or Slack the moment something fails.

Choose a platform →
{{p.mark}}{{p.name}}
Maester Packs

Extend Maester with packs.

Packs add tests, helpers and connectors that the community publishes. Every pack is scanned before it is listed and pinned to the exact files you approve.

Install-MtPack owner/repo
{{b}}
{{p.name}}
{{p.desc}}
{{p.tests}} testsby {{p.by}}
Browse all packs on packs.maester.cloud ↗
Your own checks

Write your policies as tests.

A check is one PowerShell function and a Markdown page. New-MtTest writes both, Get-MtTest validates them without a tenant, and your results land in the same report as the built-in checks.

Already have Pester tests from 2.x? They still run, and Convert-MtTest moves them over when you're ready.

Write your first test →
function Test-ContosoGuestInvites { [MaesterTest( Id = 'CONTOSO.1001', Title = 'Guest invitations are restricted', Product = 'entra', Severity = 'High', Service = 'Graph' )] param () $policy = Invoke-MtGraphRequest -RelativeUri 'policies/authorizationPolicy' $policy.allowInvitesFrom -in 'adminsAndGuestInviters', 'none' }

Checks for the services you actually run.

Need history, drift and every tenant in one place?

Maester Cloud keeps 5+ years of results, shows what changed between runs and alerts you when it does. Send your existing runs with one cmdlet. Your subscription also keeps the Maester core open and free.

[MaesterTest(
        Id = 'CIS.M365.1.1.1',
        Title = 'Ensure Administrative accounts are cloud-only',
        Product = 'microsoft-365',
        RelatedProduct = 'entra',
        Feature = 'administrative-accounts',
        Area = 'privileged-access',
        ResourceType = 'User',
        Severity = 'High',
        UserImpact = 'Low',
        ImplementationCost = 'Medium',
        Mitre = ('T1078.002', 'T1078.004', 'T1556.007'),
        Control = ('cis-m365:1.1.1', 'nist-800-53-r5:AC-6(5)'),
        Service = 'Graph',
        Author = 'soulemike',
        Contributor = 'NZLostboy'
    )]
﻿1.1.1 (L1) Ensure Administrative accounts are cloud-only

Administrative accounts are special privileged accounts that could have varying levels of access to data, users, and settings. Regular user accounts should never be utilized for administrative tasks and care should be taken, in the case of a hybrid environment, to keep administrative accounts separate from on-prem accounts. Administrative accounts should not have applications assigned so that they have no access to potentially vulnerable services (EX. email, Teams, SharePoint, etc.) and only access to perform tasks as needed for administrative purposes. **Ensure administrative accounts are not On-premises sync enabled.**

#### Rationale

In a hybrid environment, having separate accounts will help ensure that in the event of a breach in the cloud, that the breach does not affect the on-prem environment and vice versa.

#### Impact

Administrative users will need to utilize login/logout functionality to switch accounts when performing administrative tasks, which means they will not benefit from SSO. This will require a migration process from the 'daily driver' account to a dedicated admin account. Once the new admin account is created, permission sets should be migrated from the 'daily driver' account to the new admin account. This includes both M365 and Azure RBAC roles. Failure to migrate Azure RBAC roles could prevent an admin from seeing their subscriptions/resources while using their admin account.

#### Remediation action

Remediation will require first identifying the privileged accounts that are synced from onpremises and then creating a new cloud-only account for that user. Once a replacement account is established, the hybrid account should have its role reduced to that of a nonprivileged user or removed depending on the need.

#### Related links

* [Microsoft 365 Admin Center](https://admin.microsoft.com)
* [Add users and assign licenses in Microsoft 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/admin/add-users/add-users?view=o365-worldwide)
* [Step 2. Protect your Microsoft 365 privileged accounts](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/enterprise/protect-your-global-administrator-accounts?view=o365-worldwide)
* [9. Use cloud native accounts for Microsoft Entra roles](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/role-based-access-control/best-practices#9-use-cloud-native-accounts-for-microsoft-entra-roles)
* [What is Microsoft Entra?](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/fundamentals/what-is-entra)
* [Microsoft Entra built-in roles](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/role-based-access-control/permissions-reference)
* [CIS Microsoft 365 Foundations Benchmark v7.0.0 - Page 21](https://www.cisecurity.org/benchmark/microsoft_365)

  "Profile": [
    "E3 Level 1"
  ]
}

CIS.M365.1.1.1 High severity Level 1 E3 Level 1

Administrative accounts are cloud-only

Accounts that hold admin roles should exist only in Entra ID, never synced from on-premises Active Directory. This check fails when any privileged account has on-premises sync enabled.

Ask AI how to fix this View source

Why it matters

If an attacker takes over your on-premises directory, every synced account comes with them. Keeping admin accounts cloud-only means a breach of one environment does not hand over the other.

What it costs your users

Admins need a separate account for admin work and lose single sign-on for it. Move their Microsoft 365 and Azure roles to the new account, or they won't see their resources.

How to fix it

  1. Open the failed result in your Maester report to see which privileged accounts are synced.
  2. Create a cloud-only account for each of those admins.
  3. Move the admin roles to the new account, then remove them from the synced account.

How do I run only the CIS checks every night in GitHub Actions, without a client secret?

Use the Maester GitHub Action with workload identity federation, so the workflow signs in with a federated credential instead of a secret. Then limit the run to CIS in maester-config.json:

// maester-config.json in your repository { "Selection": { "Suite": ["CIS"] } }

Set include_private_tests: true on the action so it reads that file, and add a schedule trigger for the nightly run.
